```{r m4-setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", out.width = "100%")
options(width = 82)
fmt <- function(x, digits = 3) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
```

A common grade is a decision to withhold a comparison, whereas latent
equality is an event under the target distribution. These need not coincide:
unequal targets may receive a common grade, and a model may assign positive
probability to exact equality before grades are chosen. We compare losses
that treat equality differently and evaluate a finite example using
`postrank_tie_*`. The probabilities are determined by complete finite laws,
without model fitting or optimization.

## Latent equality and shared grades {#a-tie-in-the-target-is-different-from-a-tie-in-the-report}

A **latent equality** is an event such as `theta_A == theta_B` under the
supplied posterior law. It may occur with probability between zero and one,
or with probability one when two entities share the same structural target.
A **shared grade** is a reporting decision: it withholds the direction
between those entities. Shared grades do not establish equality.

Neither equal posterior means nor rounded observations establish latent
equality. Even continuous marginal distributions can have genuine ties:
if both targets are the same continuous random variable, their equality
probability is one. The relevant assumption concerns their joint law.
A rule that treats differences within a practical margin as negligible
defines a distinct decision convention; this article uses exact equality
and no margin.
The companion theory distinguishes these meanings in
[Chapter 9, “Different meanings of a tie”](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/chapters/09-targets-actions-laws.html#different-meanings-of-a-tie).

## Loss conventions at equality {#two-losses-make-different-choices-at-equality}

Take a pair of targets, with larger values having higher priority. The
ordinary weak-error loss counts a disclosed direction “A above B” as wrong
when `theta_A <= theta_B`. Withholding costs `tau`, regardless of the
latent state. The opt-in **equality-neutral loss** instead counts only
strict reversals as errors and charges withholding only when the targets
are distinct:

| Latent state | Weak: A above B | Weak: hold | Neutral: A above B | Neutral: hold |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| A > B | 0 | tau | 0 | tau |
| A = B | 1 | tau | 0 | 0 |
| A < B | 1 | tau | 1 | tau |

The neutral loss also assigns zero cost to “B above A” when the targets
are equal. Consequently, zero loss under this convention does not imply
strict superiority. Equality neutrality changes the consequences that the
loss penalizes and hence defines a different decision problem.

The default package route retains its existing weak-error meaning and
requires tie-free inputs. Its input checks do not assign an equality-neutral interpretation
to atoms. The weak-loss column below is
therefore calculated directly for illustration; a positive-tie law is
passed to the separate tie-aware constructor. The two definitions and
their difference are derived in
[Chapter 11, “An equality-neutral extension of directional loss”](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/chapters/11-multicriteria-loss.html#sec-tie-aware-loss).

## A finite two-entity law {#specify-a-complete-two-entity-law}

Consider a law in which B has score 1 with probability one and A has scores
0, 1 and 2 with probabilities .1, .4 and .5. The three states specify the
complete posterior for this example, rather than a Monte Carlo sample.

```{r m4-law}
library(postrank)
states <- lapply(c(0, 1, 2), function(a)
  matrix(c(a, 1), nrow = 2,
    dimnames = list(entity = c("A", "B"), criterion = "score")))
masses <- c(1L, 4L, 5L)
law_table <- data.frame(A = c(0, 1, 2), B = 1,
  Probability = masses / sum(masses))
knitr::kable(law_table)
```

The exact-law constructor requires integer state values, integer mass
numerators and a common denominator. Exact coefficient arithmetic uses
the optional `gmp` package. The following helper supplies the declarations
for the specified examples to `as_postrank_tie_draws()`. In applications,
the target and model descriptions must correspond to the scientific
quantities and assumptions of the analysis.

<details>
<summary>Construct the finite input, including its target and equality declarations</summary>

```{r m4-constructor}
finite_input <- function(states, masses, description) {
  ids <- rownames(states[[1]])
  criteria <- colnames(states[[1]])
  payload <- list(
    schema_version = "tie-aware-input-0.1",
    input_kind = "exact_finite_posterior",
    dependence_mode = "joint_model",
    requested_functional = "expected_rank_loss",
    entity_ids = ids, criterion_ids = criteria,
    targets = lapply(criteria, function(k) list(
      criterion_id = k, estimand = paste("Specified", k, "target"),
      entity_population = "Fictional entities in the displayed law",
      time_reference = "No observation period; mathematical example",
      units = "Illustrative score units", source_transform = "Identity",
      identification_basis = "Defined by the complete listed states",
      orientation = "higher_priority")),
    context = list(cohort_id = "m4-example", data_version = "1",
      data_conditioning = "No observations; the listed law is stipulated",
      model_summary = description),
    identification = list(status = "identified_declared",
      note = "The mathematical targets are specified, not empirically identified"),
    tie_policy = list(rule = "equality_neutral", declared = TRUE,
      justification = "Equality in a listed state is genuine target equality",
      observed_tie_action = "accept_declared_exact_equality"),
    provenance = list(producer = "M4 vignette", artifact_id = "specified-law",
      artifact_hash = digest::digest(list(states, masses), algo = "sha256"),
      construction_note = "Complete finite law; no sampling or rounding",
      created_at = format(Sys.time(), tz = "UTC", format = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")),
    equality = list(basis = "exact_finite_law",
      justification = "Check equality over every positive-mass state",
      criterion_classes = NULL),
    finite_law = list(denominator = sum(masses),
      value_representation = "safe_integer",
      states = lapply(seq_along(states), function(s) list(
        state_id = paste0("state-", s), mass_numerator = masses[s],
        theta = states[[s]])),
      law_definition = description, not_empirical_posterior_relabeling = TRUE)
  )
  as_postrank_tie_draws(payload)
}
```

</details>

```{r m4-probabilities}
input <- finite_input(states, masses,
  "B is 1; A is 0, 1, or 2 with masses 1/10, 4/10, 5/10")
pw <- postrank_tie_pairwise(input)
probabilities <- data.frame(
  Event = c("A < B", "A = B", "A != B", "B < A"),
  Probability = c(pw$b["A", "B", "score"], pw$t["A", "B", "score"],
    pw$d["A", "B", "score"], pw$b["B", "A", "score"])
)
knitr::kable(probabilities)
```

Here `b[i, j, k]` is the strict error probability for disclosing `i` above
`j`; `t` is equality probability and `d` is distinctness probability.
Off-diagonal entries satisfy `b[i,j,k] + b[j,i,k] = d[i,j,k]`, not generally
one. In this example .1 + .5 = .6; using `1 - .1` for the reverse strict
error would incorrectly include the equality mass. Diagonal entries are
`NA` because an entity is not compared with itself.

## Evaluation of the three actions {#evaluate-directions-and-withholding}

The three possible ordered reports for two entities can be evaluated
directly. At `tau = .25`, their neutral risks are as follows:

```{r m4-actions}
tau <- .25
actions <- list(`A above B` = c(A = 1L, B = 2L),
  `B above A` = c(A = 2L, B = 1L), Hold = c(A = 1L, B = 1L))
evaluations <- lapply(actions, postrank_tie_evaluate,
  pairwise = pw, weights = c(score = 1), tau = tau)
p <- masses / sum(masses)
weak_risk <- c(sum(p * (law_table$A <= law_table$B)),
  sum(p * (law_table$B <= law_table$A)), tau)
action_table <- data.frame(Action = names(actions), Weak_loss = weak_risk,
  Neutral_loss = vapply(evaluations, function(x) x$primary_risk, numeric(1)))
knitr::kable(action_table, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

Under neutral loss, A above B has risk .1, compared with .25 × .6 = .15
for withholding, and is therefore preferred. Weak loss favors withholding
because the disclosed error includes the .4 equality mass. Enumeration
exhausts the two-entity action space, so no numerical optimality bound is
required. For more entities, individually preferred pairwise actions may
fail to define a coherent grading.

For several entities and criteria, let `E_k` sum strict-error probabilities
over disclosed pairs, `D_k` sum their distinctness probabilities, and
`T_k` sum distinctness probabilities over **all** unordered pairs.
With criterion weights summing to one, write
`E_w = sum(w * E_k)`, `D = sum(w * D_k)` and `T = sum(w * T_k)`.
The neutral risk is

\[
R = \frac{E_w + \tau(T-D)}{M}
  = R_0 + \frac{E_w-\tau D}{M},
\qquad R_0 = \frac{\tau T}{M},\qquad M=\binom{n}{2}.
\]

Consequently, the all-withhold baseline is `R0`, generally below `tau`.
The centered objective `raw_Z` subtracts `tau * D`, not `tau * N`.
The evaluator checks risk from the disclosed and withheld event masses;
the identity can also be checked directly:

```{r m4-risk-identity}
forward <- evaluations[["A above B"]]
c(direct = forward$primary_risk,
  baseline_plus_centered = forward$R0 + forward$raw_Z / forward$M,
  all_withhold = evaluations$Hold$primary_risk)
```

## Disclosure and distinctness denominators {#read-the-denominator-as-carefully-as-the-numerator}

`N/M` counts the fraction of pairs assigned different grades. It does not
discount possible latent equality. `D/T` measures the fraction of weighted
distinct-comparison opportunity disclosed. Criterion-specific `E_over_N`
and `E_over_D` divide the same strict-error count by different quantities:

```{r m4-denominators}
denominators <- do.call(rbind, lapply(evaluations, function(x)
  data.frame(N = x$N, D = x$D, T = x$T,
    `E/N` = unname(x$E_over_N), `E/D` = unname(x$E_over_D),
    `D/T` = x$D_over_T, check.names = FALSE)))
knitr::kable(denominators, digits = 3)
```

For A above B, .1 strict errors per raw pair becomes .1/.6 = 1/6 per
distinct comparison. These are ratios of posterior expected counts, not
expectations of state-by-state error ratios. With several criteria,
`E_over_D` uses each criterion's `D_k`; the scalar `D` is its weighted
summary. In the companion theory this weighted quantity is denoted
`Q_w`, avoiding a notation collision with an earlier weak-error count.

For comparison, consider equality with probability one and an action
that withholds the comparison:

```{r m4-zero-denominators}
equal_pw <- postrank_tie_pairwise(finite_input(states[2], 1L,
  "A and B both equal 1 with probability one"))
equal_hold <- postrank_tie_evaluate(actions$Hold, equal_pw,
  weights = c(score = 1), tau = tau)
equal_hold[c("N", "D", "T", "E_over_N", "E_over_D", "D_over_T", "R0")]
```

All three denominators `N`, `D` and `T` are zero, giving `NA` for their
ratios. Zero risk in this example follows from certain equality and
provides no evidence for a strict order. A disclosure with `D = 0` could
also have zero strict error; the equality guard described below restricts
such disclosures.

## Reduction under zero equality probability {#check-the-zero-tie-case}

For a separate comparison, move all equality mass to the state A=2, B=1.
The new complete law has masses .1 and .9 and no equality. Strict and weak
errors then coincide; `d = 1`, `D = N`, `T = M`, and `R0 = tau`.

```{r m4-no-ties}
no_tie <- postrank_tie_pairwise(finite_input(states[c(1, 3)], c(1L, 9L),
  "A is 0 or 2 with masses 1/10 and 9/10; B is 1; equality is impossible"))
ordinary <- postrank_probabilities(no_tie$b,
  event = "directional_error", zero_ties = TRUE, margin = 0,
  source = list(kind = "analytic_reference",
    description = "Probabilities summed over the displayed two-state law",
    conditioning = "Complete stipulated law; no sampled approximation"),
  targets = c(score = "Higher specified score has higher priority"))
no_tie_table <- data.frame(Action = names(actions),
  Ordinary = vapply(actions, function(g)
    postrank_evaluate(g, ordinary, c(score = 1), tau)$primary_risk, numeric(1)),
  Neutral = vapply(actions, function(g)
    postrank_tie_evaluate(g, no_tie, c(score = 1), tau)$primary_risk, numeric(1)))
knitr::kable(no_tie_table, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

The losses agree for every action when all positive-weight criteria have
zero pairwise equality probability and the action domain and other settings
coincide. Zero-weight criteria do not affect the identity. This mathematical
agreement does not require identical floating-point representations or the
same numerical choice among multiple minimizers.

## The same-grade constraint for identical active profiles {#keep-identical-active-profiles-in-the-same-grade}

Positive equality probability for one pair is weaker than equality with
probability one. The guard uses the latter: if two entities are equal in
every state on **every positive-weight criterion**, they must receive the
same grade in a released tie-aware solution.

Consider one certain state with a shared attribute and an individual one:

```{r m4-guard-law}
profile_state <- matrix(c(2, 2, 0, 0, 1, 2), nrow = 3,
  dimnames = list(entity = c("A", "B", "C"),
    criterion = c("shared", "individual")))
knitr::kable(profile_state)
profile_pw <- postrank_tie_pairwise(finite_input(list(profile_state), 1L,
  "One certain state with the displayed shared and individual attributes"))
split <- c(A = 1L, B = 2L, C = 3L)
only_shared <- postrank_tie_evaluate(split, profile_pw,
  c(shared = 1, individual = 0), tau)
both_active <- postrank_tie_evaluate(split, profile_pw,
  c(shared = .5, individual = .5), tau)
data.frame(Weights = c("1 / 0", ".5 / .5"),
  Guard_satisfied = c(only_shared$guard_satisfied, both_active$guard_satisfied))
```

A and B must share a grade when only `shared` has positive weight. When
both criteria are active, their different individual values remove that
requirement. The evaluator deliberately permits scoring a guard-violating
action for comparison; a finite risk alone does not make it admissible.

The problem constructor enforces the guard while keeping all original
entities and pair multiplicities:

```{r m4-problem}
problem <- postrank_tie_problem(profile_pw,
  weights = c(shared = 1, individual = 0), tau = tau, G_max = 3L)
problem$guard$classes
problem$M
```

There are still three entities and three pairs, even when A and B must
share a grade. Replacing them with one unweighted representative would
change the problem. For the full weighted **at-most-G** family without
additional restrictions, a global minimizer satisfying this guard exists:
moving identical profiles to their least costly currently occupied grade
cannot increase loss or the number of grades. This is an existence result,
not a claim that every optimum obeys the guard or that any arbitrary merge
preserves risk. See
[“Same-grade guard for identical active profiles”](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/chapters/11-multicriteria-loss.html#a-guard-for-identical-active-profiles)
for the argument and its restrictions.

For Monte Carlo input, structural equality classes must be declared and
checked against the retained values. Coincidence in the sampled draws is
insufficient to establish these classes. For a complete finite law, they
are determined by all positive-mass states. If ties arise from rounding
continuous draws, full-precision values are required; jitter and numerical
tolerances would alter the comparison being defined.

## Supported inputs and decision problems {#use-the-supported-mode-deliberately}

The current mode supports complete exact finite laws and joint equal-weight
IID or MCMC draws. It supports weighted at-most-G problems with the guard,
and native HiGHS or Gurobi solution through `label_mip`. The following call
is optional and is not executed by this article:

```{r m4-optional-solve, eval=FALSE}
fit <- postrank_tie_solve(problem, backend = "highs",
  control = postrank_control(strategy = "label_mip", time_limit = 30,
    threads = 1L, seed = 1304L))
```

`q` error budgets, minimax, exact-G, and staged solving are unsupported in
this mode. Criterionwise inputs and typed Gaussian/mixture coefficients
are also outside its current input paths. The guard's weighted at-most-G
argument does not automatically extend to those other constraints or
objectives.

Tie-aware objects provide `print()`, `format()` and `summary()` methods,
with results stored in `grade`, `evaluation` and `objective`. The legacy
accessors, baseline comparisons, HTML reports and plots are unavailable
for this object family, as are Monte Carlo diagnostics, uniform IID bounds,
regret bounds and protection envelopes. These restrictions are listed by
`postrank_tie_capabilities()`. Exact rational coefficients also leave
subsequent floating-point losses and solver bounds subject to numerical
error.

The definitions here follow JoonHo Lee (2026), *Decisions from Noisy
Multidimensional Indicators: Theory, Evidence, and Posterior Grading*,
version 3: Chapter 9, “Grade actions and disclosed comparisons”; Chapter
11, “An equality-neutral extension of directional loss,” especially
“Risk identity and relation to the weak-error loss” and “Same-grade guard
for identical active profiles”; and
[Appendix D, “Equality-neutral implementation and capability limits”](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/appendices/D-package-correspondence.html#sec-package-tie-aware).
The software limits above were
also checked against the current package. The ordinary loss is defined in
[Ranking, grades and loss](m1-ranking-and-loss.html), input assumptions in
[Posterior inputs](m3-posterior-inputs.html), and numerical statuses in
[Computing grades](m5-computing-grades.html).
